title: Modeling K-12 After Northeastern University and Link Ventures
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard uses a remarkable detail—a fourteen-year-old who built a foundation model pitching a venture fund designed for college graduates—to expose the structural mismatch between what K-12 schools know how to do and what the AI economy actually demands. Schools understand how to manage young people; venture funds understand how to support founders; each holds what the other is missing. Bauschard argues that while schools have spent two years debating phone bans and AI prohibitions, the relevant question has moved on: containment is not the skill the AI economy will reward. Drawing on Northeastern's model of work-integrated learning and Link Ventures' community of support, he outlines what schools could build—real projects, mentors, alumni networks, demo days—if they chose to stop waiting.
points: A fourteen-year-old founder building a foundation model is the forcing function: venture funds built for college-age founders are now encountering middle schoolers, and neither schools nor funds know how to handle the overlap.
Schools and funds hold complementary assets—schools manage young people, funds develop founders—making partnership a logical structural fit that remains almost entirely unexplored.
Phone bans and AI prohibitions are containment strategies that answer the wrong question; the AI economy will not reward the skill of complying with restrictions.
Northeastern's model of deeply integrated external experience—alumni networks, real employers, mentors, demo days—is replicable at the K-12 level and represents what Bauschard calls 'the build list.'
The same student with the same laptop looks like a discipline problem to one institution and a founder to another—the difference is institutional orientation, not the student.
quotes: 'Our whole model is geared up for young, but now we're talking about another level of young. We have some thinking to do.'

Schools know how to manage students this young—it is the one thing they indisputably know—but not founders. The fund knows founders—the capital, the mentors, the network, the path from pitch to company—but not fourteen-year-olds.
Here is what American secondary education spent the last two years arguing about while a fourteen-year-old trained a foundation model: where students may keep their phones.

He calls the reflex what it is: 'our first reaction was a protectionist reaction,' built on 'the students will be cheating.' And he goes further: higher education 'divorced ourselves from the real world.'
Same kid, same laptop—one institution sees a discipline problem, the other sees a founder.
